title: Ward CO Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Ward wells have a 300-foot median depth, 7 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $25,500-$42,000.
h1: Wells in Ward, Colorado: Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land or a home near Ward means dealing with mountain bedrock, variable well depths, and a limited amount of water-level data. Records within 5 miles show a median well depth of 300 feet and a median reported yield of 7.0 gallons per minute.

Most permitted wells serve domestic or household use. The local records point to fractured granite and other fractured crystalline rock, not Denver Basin groundwater. That makes neighboring well records, the permit file, and a careful site review important before you commit to a lot.

sections.heading: Ward well depth follows fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
Ward wells have a median reported depth of 300 feet. The middle half runs from 126 to 438 feet, while the 90th percentile reaches 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 1,428 feet. For a drilling bid, that spread matters more than the median alone: a contractor may need to price a substantially deeper hole if the first water-bearing fractures are not productive.

Depths are distributed across the area. Nineteen percent of reported wells are under 100 feet, 30% are 100 to 300 feet, 38% are 300 to 600 feet, and 13% exceed 600 feet. Permit records name unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers for 638 wells, with only a few identifying Fractured Granite or Fractured Crystalline aquifers.

sections.heading: What Ward wells produce for a household
sections.html:
The median reported yield is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 5.0 and 9.0 gallons per minute. That is a useful local benchmark for a home, but it is not a guarantee for an untested parcel. A yield test and storage system still determine how comfortably a house can handle peak demand.

Five percent of reported wells produce under 1 gallon per minute, 19% produce 1 to 5 gallons per minute, 68% produce 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 8% produce more than 15 gallons per minute. The low-yield group is small but important. Ask for the well completion report, pump information, and any long-term production or recovery test.

sections.heading: Water levels show limited but important change
sections.html:
Only 29 wells in the records report a static water level, so the local water-level sample is much smaller than the depth and yield samples. Across those reports, the median depth to water is 50 feet, with the middle half from 18 to 100 feet below the surface.

The decade figures move from a median of 52 feet below surface in the 2010s to 72 feet in the 2020s. That suggests deeper measured water levels in the newer records, but it does not prove a broad groundwater decline because the sample is limited and measurements may come from different wells and conditions. Have a qualified professional measure the existing well before closing.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers around Ward
sections.html:
Ward has a long permit record, with 661 wells in the Colorado DWR records and 405 recorded as constructed. Permits were issued in every decade listed: 7 in the 1950s, 10 in the 1960s, 109 in the 1970s, 95 in the 1980s, 130 in the 1990s, 97 in the 2000s, 69 in the 2010s, and 30 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most active drillers in these records are Ground Water Systems Inc. (Wilson, Richard R.) with 151 permits, Ingram Drilling Inc. (Ingram, Stephen E.) with 73, and Norris & Sons (Norris, T A) with 25. Those records show local activity, not a guarantee of current availability or quality. Confirm licensing, scope, and references directly before hiring.

sections.heading: Estimated drilling cost in Ward's bedrock
sections.html:
Ward ground is fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 300-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $19,500 to $30,000.

A finished well is more than the hole. Including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, the estimated total is about $25,500 to $42,000 at the median depth. A 600-foot well would require a separate bid, and the final cost can change with access, casing, grout, water testing, site conditions, and whether the well reaches a productive fracture. Request an itemized proposal rather than comparing only a per-foot rate.

sections.heading: Ward risks: water quality, dry holes, and the building site
sections.html:
Fractured rock can produce a good well, but water-bearing fractures are unevenly distributed. Low yield or a dry hole remains a site-specific risk even when nearby wells look favorable. Review neighboring completion reports, pump tests, and static water levels instead of relying on a countywide average.

Within about 10 miles, the map includes 11 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 887 historic mine features, and 59 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped features do not establish contamination at a particular lot, but they justify testing the well water and checking the property's relationship to mines and cleanup areas. Also confirm septic setbacks, suitable soil, driveway access, and a buildable house location before drilling.

sections.heading: Before buying or building near Ward
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado DWR permit and construction records for the property and nearby wells. Compare locations around Hidden Lake, Bark Ranch, Gold Hill, St. Ann Highlands, Sugarloaf, and Bonanza Mountain Estates only as local context; each parcel still needs its own review. Confirm the permitted use, well construction, pump capacity, and any restrictions that affect the planned home.

For vacant land, make the well location, access route, septic area, and electrical plan work together before construction begins. For an existing home, test the water, measure the static level, inspect the pressure system, and ask how the well performs during dry periods. A well producing 7.0 gallons per minute may be adequate, but the property-specific records matter more than the median.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Ward, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Ward is 300 feet. The middle half runs from 126 to 438 feet, and the 90th percentile is 600 feet. Nineteen percent are under 100 feet, while 13% exceed 600 feet. Fractured mountain bedrock makes the depth for a new well difficult to predict from averages alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Ward, CO?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 300-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $19,500 to $30,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $25,500 to $42,000. Deeper drilling, difficult access, casing, grout, and site conditions can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Ward?
faq.a: The median reported well yield near Ward is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 5.0 to 9.0 gallons per minute. Five percent of reported wells produce under 1 gallon per minute. Because the area uses fractured-bedrock aquifers, a nearby well does not guarantee the same result. Review the completion report and obtain a yield test.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Ward, Colorado?
faq.a: The permit records do not establish that every Ward well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles are 11 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 887 historic mine features, and 59 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the individual well for appropriate contaminants, especially when a property is near mines or mapped cleanup areas, and retest when conditions change.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping around Ward?
faq.a: Reported median static water levels were 52 feet below surface in the 2010s and 72 feet in the 2020s. That points to deeper measurements in the newer records, but only 29 wells report static water levels, so it is not proof of a region-wide decline. Have the property's well measured and review its history before relying on the trend.
